stepInfo.context: Context is the ground everything stands on: who you are, what you offer, for whom — and the market you move in. Every later recommendation from George rests on these facts; without solid context, values, archetype and tagline would be guesses instead of derivations.
stepInfo.pvm: The compass of your brand: the purpose says why you exist. The vision, where you are headed. The mission, how you get there. Together they are the yardstick for every decision — from the price list to the Instagram post.
stepInfo.architecture: Brand architecture sorts your family of brands: does everything appear under one brand, do products carry names of their own — and who lends trust to whom? From three switches George derives a model and turns it into a naming rule every future offer can be measured against.
stepInfo.values: Values are the rules of conduct of your brand: they say how you decide when it gets uncomfortable. In the Brand Foundation they are the hinge between purpose (why you exist) and archetype & voice (how you sound) — every later design and copy decision is measured against them.
stepInfo.archetype: The archetype gives your brand a recognisable character — a pattern people understand intuitively (the sage, the explorer, the caregiver …). The voice derives from it: how you sound, what you talk about and what you never do. That way everyone on the team writes as if the same person were writing.
stepInfo.manifesto: The manifesto condenses the whole foundation into one text with a stance — the piece you can read out loud: on the website, in the pitch, when onboarding new people. It grows out of purpose, values and voice, not the other way round.
stepInfo.verbal: The tagline is the one line next to your name; the messaging is the set of core messages behind it — what you tell whom so it sticks. Both build on the foundation: without clarified values, every tagline sounds arbitrary.
stepInfo.naming: Whether it is a new brand or a test bench for the existing name: here the name is measured against the foundation — does it fit purpose, values and archetype? Plus the sober checks: is it available, is it pronounceable, does it work in English too?
stepInfo.result: The result bundles every confirmed decision of the foundation into your brand document — with a direction for everything that follows. From here you move on to design, copy and the public face; and the more honest the chapters before, the more the result can carry.

c.discovery1: When a customer recommended us before their own project was even finished.
c.discovery2: When we took a job nobody believed in — just for the money.

d.party: Listens first, asks smart questions — then tells the story everyone remembers.
d.never: Preachy — we explain without talking down.
d.admired: Patagonia — they speak their mind even when it costs them revenue.
d.emotion: Relief: finally someone who genuinely takes care of it.
d.vocabulary: Never: cheap, deal, mega offer — we do not talk like a flyer.

e.warmup1: That everyone promises the same thing and nobody delivers it.
e.warmup2: How much experience goes into a result that looks simple.

f.taste: Vitra, Patagonia, Aesop — short, distinctive, memorable without explanation.
f.noGos: No made-up English words, nothing with global or 24 in the name.

b.purpose: Purpose is the WHY: the reason you exist beyond making money. Vision is the WHERE TO, mission is the HOW — three sentences, three jobs. Patagonia's purpose does not sell jackets; it wants to save the planet.
b.vision: The vision describes the world once you have succeeded — a picture, not a target figure. It may sit ten years out and still has to give direction today.
b.mission: The mission says what you do every day to get there — concrete enough that a new colleague could act on it. Purpose is why, vision is where to, mission is how.
b.positioningCategory: Positioning is the place you claim in someone's head: a category, and the people for whom you are the first choice within it. Without a category people still compare you — just without your say in it.

b2.model: Four models: branded house (one brand carries everything), sub-brands, endorsed brands, house of brands (brands without a visible parent). Each buys a different kind of trust, and each has a price.

c.candidates: Values are rules of behaviour that are allowed to cost money — not poster words. Survey after survey finds that most employees cannot name their own company's values; that is what happens when the words were picked for their sound.
c.final: Three to five is the working range: fewer says nothing, more nobody remembers. Take the ones you would defend in a bad week, not the ones that read well.

d.pairs: The archetype is your brand's character — it steers voice, imagery and effect. You don't pick it off a list: it comes out of comparisons, because a decision between two feelings is more honest than a menu of twelve.
d.primary: Twelve archetypes in four groups; you get a primary and a secondary one. The primary sets the tone, the secondary keeps it from turning into a cliché.
d.gapReveal: Here your self-image meets the picture your current appearance sends out. A gap is not a mistake — it is the most useful thing on this page, and it gets named plainly instead of smoothed over.

e.statements: A manifesto takes a stand: it should attract the right people and put off the wrong ones. The openers are scaffolding — cross out whatever sounds borrowed and keep what you would say out loud.
e.manifesto: A mission explains, a manifesto commits. It is written to be read aloud, so shorter and sharper almost always wins.

f.nameType: There are nine kinds of names — descriptive, invented, metaphorical and so on. Choose the kind first, then brainstorm: a mixed list always collapses into the safest option.
f.taste: The name is the most repeated element of a brand — it has to be sayable, memorable and protectable. What you love about other people's names says more about your taste than any list of adjectives.
f.checks: The more invented a name, the more protectable it is. What you see here are indicators from public registries and from DNS — general information, not legal advice. Talk to a trademark lawyer before you commit.

a1.title: The first sentence belongs to you alone
a1.next: Write the first sentence so that no competitor could sign it — in the relaunch that is the first building block.

a2.title: Name and claim are unmistakable
a2.next: Check whether your claim states something instead of naming a category — your brand advisor asks that first.

a3.title: No stock phrases in the opening
a3.next: Replace every stock phrase with a concrete fact: a number, a name, an example.

a4.title: A recognisable point of view
a4.next: Write down one sentence you would say even when not everybody likes it — that becomes your stance.

a5.title: Your own imagery instead of stock
a5.next: Collect three motifs from your real working day; they carry more than any bought picture.

b1.title: Favicon and preview image in place
b1.next: Add both — it is the smallest piece of brand there is, and it travels everywhere.

b2.title: Clean heading hierarchy
b2.next: Give the page exactly one main heading and a clear order beneath it.

b3.title: Alt texts describe a visual world
b3.next: Describe in the alt texts what can be seen — you sort out your imagery along the way.

b4.title: Colour and theme meta set
b4.next: Put your brand colour into the page head so browsers and apps pick it up.

b5.title: Words and pictures belong together
b5.next: Put texts and motifs side by side and cut whatever could come from another brand.

c1.title: One tone across the whole page
c1.next: Settle on one form of address and one register and keep it — the wizard records it as a rule.

c2.title: Title, preview and heading say the same
c2.next: Align the three lines; it is the same sentence in three places.

c3.title: The promise at the top carries the page
c3.next: Check section by section whether it delivers the promise from the opening.

c4.title: Language declared and consistent
c4.next: Set the language attribute to match the text — for search engines and for screen readers.

c5.title: The brand name is written consistently
c5.next: Fix one spelling and keep it everywhere, including inside running text.

d1.title: One clear call to action
d1.next: Put an action with a verb at the top — book, ask, try — instead of a vague more.

d2.title: The next step is unambiguous
d2.next: Cut the side paths until one main action is left.

d3.title: Findability: title and description
d3.next: Write title and description at a good length — they are your appearance in search.

d4.title: Structured data for search and AI
d4.next: Add organisation and website as structured data so answer engines quote you correctly.

d5.title: Contact and trust are visible
d5.next: Show who stands behind the brand and make contact reachable in one click.

e1.title: Understandable in ten seconds
e1.next: Say what you offer in the first paragraph, without a run-up.

e2.title: Who it is made for
e2.next: Name your audience — in the wizard that is a building block of its own.

e3.title: A short, active core sentence
e3.next: Cut your core sentence to twenty words at most, with an active verb.

e4.title: Recognisable differentiation
e4.next: Say plainly what you do differently — without naming the competition.

e5.title: Little jargon
e5.next: Swap long technical words for the words your customers use.

f1.title: The page speaks to a feeling
f1.next: Alongside the service, tell what it changes for people.

f2.title: A story or an origin
f2.next: Write three sentences on why you exist — that carries half the brand.

f3.title: A human voice instead of officialese
f3.next: Speak as people: we instead of one, concrete images, short sentences.

f4.title: A moment worth passing on
f4.next: Allow yourselves one wilful line — one is enough.

f5.title: The tone fits the category
f5.next: Check that your tone fits what you offer — and the people who buy it.

checkPage.seoTitle: Brand check — audit your brand presence and get your Brand Score
checkPage.seoDescription: Free brand check: enter your website, 40 criteria across eight categories, a Brand Score from 0 to 100 and the three most important findings with evidence. No account, in under a minute.

hero.title: How strong is your brand?
hero.lead: Enter your website and know in under a minute where your brand presence stands today — Brand Score, eight categories, three findings with evidence.

what.title: The outside view of your brand presence
what.body: We read your homepage — exactly what any visitor sees — and assess it against 40 criteria in eight categories. Out comes a Brand Score from 0 to 100, eight category scores and the three most important findings, each with the evidence it rests on.
what.honest: This is a maturity level, not a report card: it says where you stand today and what would be next.
what.f1Body: Each with a fixed rule from 0 to 2. None of it is taste.
what.f2Body: From distinctiveness to craft, each with its own weight.
what.f3Body: One number with a band that you can compare with today a year from now.

why.title: Your brand takes shape in other minds
why.body1: A brand is not what you say about yourselves, it is what arrives with everyone else. That view of your own presence is the one you never get: you know the intent behind every sentence, a visitor only knows the sentence.
why.body2: The check takes that view. It does not judge your taste, it checks whether your intent makes it out — and every finding says what it rests on.

value.eyebrow: What you get out of it
value.title: Three findings you can start with tomorrow
value.v1Body: Every finding carries its quote or its measurement and the next step. You do not have to believe anyone, you can read it.
value.v2Body: No sign-up, no email address, no call-back request. Enter the address, look at the result.
value.v3Body: The result has an address of its own. Send it to your team or your management instead of building slides.

basis.title: Eight categories, forty criteria
basis.lead: The same criteria every branding here is built with. The weights are fixed before your page is read.
basis.note: 16 criteria are computed, 24 are assessed by a brand expert — every judgement with evidence.
basis.lockedNote: What cannot be checked from the outside we do not guess: it drops out of the calculation instead of counting as zero.

features.title: What else the check does
features.f1Body: The same address returns the same stored check within a week — reproducible instead of random.
features.f2Body: If you like, your check joins the list of all audited presences. Without the checkbox it stays private.
features.f3Body: Two results side by side, category by category — like two cards against each other.
features.f4Body: Run the check again after a relaunch and see both states next to each other.

next.title: The findings become the order of the work
next.body: Your brand advisor already knows your presence by then — you start with the result instead of from zero. And your new branding can go through the same check later on.
next.brandsHint: You are signed in: your brands are in the dashboard.

faq.title: What you want to know first
faq.q1A: Your homepage only: the visible text and the details in the page head, at most 20,000 characters. No login area, no subpages, no third-party data.
faq.q2A: We store the audited address, the score and the evidence so your result stays reachable under its link. The check needs no email address.
faq.q3A: Because that is where the brand decides: the homepage is the first impression. It is also the one place we can treat the same way on every website — only then are two results comparable at all.
faq.q4Q: How often may I run it?
faq.q4A: Three checks a day per connection. The same address returns the same stored result within seven days and does not count again.
faq.q5Q: Can I take my website out of the ranking?
faq.q5A: Yes. A check only enters the ranking with the checkbox, and anyone who runs a website can have its entry removed at any time — write to us and we hide it.
faq.q6A: Some things cannot be checked from the outside. Instead of guessing we mark them and leave them out of the calculation: they count neither as a point nor as a deduction.

teaser.title: How strong is your brand — seen from the outside?
teaser.body: 40 criteria, eight categories, a Brand Score from 0 to 100 with the three most important findings. No account, in under a minute.
teaser.sampleNote: This is what a result looks like: one number with a band and eight categories below it.
